"Proof of use" as a requirement for open source contributions?
description:
As an open source maintainer, I get a lot of AI slop PRs. Some of these have genuine value. Most address edge cases that almost never occur in real life. It's not that they're not fixing real problems, it's that they're fixing problems that nobody is ever likely to encounter.

I'm experimenting with "proof of use" as a requirement for submissions. Specifically, you need to show me that your project that depends on my project before I'll look at your PR.

"Proof of use" can be an existing open source project that imports mine (show me the git history!) or a clear description starting with "in our closed source project in production, we found that...".

The specific problem that I want to address is ensuring that contributions from people genuinely depending on my software are handled, while filtering out the OpenClaw/Github green square farming/drive-by LLM noise.

What are lobste.rs's thoughts on this?

Maxanti - A logic puzzle
description:
I vibecoded a puzzle game for a math professor friend of mine as a birthday present. He seemed to like it, so I am sharing it with all you guys as well. My friend enjoy figuring things out by himself, for him it's part of the puzzle, so the manual link provided below was not initially given to him.

The game has no ads, no cookies, no analytics - the server doesn't even write an access log. That being said, I have really no idea of what's going on inside the code, I have not read any of it or done any proper review. The model used was Fable 5.2 on high effort, and the project was done in an afternoon and ended up using about 11m tokens. It was designed as a mobile first PWA project using a Bauhaus inspired theme. The size of the download is about 200KB.

The game: https://maxanti.com

The manual: https://maxanti.com/help

GLHF

title: Formal Operations Specifications for Reliable System Management
description: Abstract: Large-scale production systems are largely operated by management software like Kubernetes operators and increasingly by AI agents. Production systems have diverse functionalities, interfaces, and fault-tolerance properties; hence, their management semantics are complex and less standard. Today, management-plane software is largely implemented based on experience and documents of the managed systems, where correct management is a best effort. We advocate for the practice of writing formal operations specification (FOS) as a formal contract to precisely describe expected behaviors of the production system and to enable systematic checking and verification of management-plane software and agents. We argue that the FOS should be part of standard system interface to enable reliable system management. We suggest that every production system include a FOS and share our experience of writing FOSes for real-world systems; we show that writing and maintaining a FOS is affordable and can potentially be automated
